sections.title: What Blood Pressure Checks Are
sections.proseHtml:
A pharmacy blood pressure check measures your reading, explains it in plain language, and helps you understand sensible next steps.

Regular blood pressure checks help identify raised readings early, when lifestyle changes or a GP review may be most useful.

The pharmacy team can explain the reading in plain language and provide appropriate general guidance.

Blood pressure is recorded as systolic over diastolic (mmHg). One raised check warrants follow-up discussion — not immediate diagnosis.

sections.title: Who Should Consider Blood Pressure Checks
sections.proseHtml:
Why Blood Pressure Matters High blood pressure often has no symptoms but can increase stroke, heart disease and kidney risk over time. Risk factors such as age over 40, family history, diabetes and lifestyle habits influence how often screening is useful. Community pharmacy checks offer accessible measurement and clear explanation of your reading. Do I need to speak to a GP? Can lifestyle changes help? How often should I be checked? What does my reading mean?

Understanding Hypertension Risk Hypertension frequently causes no obvious warning signs, which is why routine measurement matters. Cardiovascular risk rises when readings stay elevated — early detection supports timely discussion with a GP when needed. Silent symptoms and hidden risk Stroke and heart disease links Kidney health awareness When to seek urgent care

When Screening Helps Screening is especially valuable for adults over 40, those with family history of hypertension, and people managing diabetes or high cardiovascular risk. One reading does not diagnose hypertension. Age and family history Diabetes and smoking Salt intake and weight Pharmacy checks and GP care

Cardiovascular Health Basics Blood pressure reflects how hard the heart and vessels work. Sustained high readings warrant further assessment — a pharmacy check identifies raised readings and explains what they may mean in plain language. Systolic and diastolic explained White-coat effect Repeat measurement importance GP and pharmacy roles

Why Regular Checks Matter Untreated hypertension increases long-term harm even without symptoms. Regular pharmacy screening can help you notice changes early and decide when a GP review is appropriate. Why routine checks help Lifestyle advice scope Limits of a single reading Safety-netting guidance

sections.title: Eligibility and suitability
sections.proseHtml:
Who Should Have A Check

Suitability is confirmed individually. Adults over 40, those with risk factors, or people due a routine review may benefit — but diagnosis requires GP assessment, not one pharmacy reading alone.

  • Age over 40
  • Family history
  • Diabetes
  • Previous raised readings
  • Lifestyle risk factors

Who The Service Suits

The check suits people seeking screening, monitoring between GP reviews, or advice after their own readings. Emergency symptoms such as chest pain need urgent care, not a pharmacy check alone.

  • Routine screening
  • Monitoring known risk
  • Discussing your own readings
  • Not for acute emergencies

Who This May Suit

Individual assessment confirms whether a pharmacy check is appropriate. Contact the pharmacy to ask how the service is arranged and whether it suits your situation.

  • Individual suitability
  • Pregnancy and complex cases
  • When GP review is better first
  • Contact before you visit

Before You Get In Touch

Share relevant medical history and medicines when you speak to the team. The pharmacist confirms scope and advises you to contact a GP or urgent care when symptoms fall outside pharmacy screening.

  • Medicines list
  • Recent symptoms
  • Previous BP readings
  • Ongoing GP treatment

sections.title: What happens during the consultation
sections.proseHtml:
1. How The Check Works A routine check covers measurement and a plain-language discussion of your reading. Each step is explained, with advice on when further medical review may help. Rest before measurement Arm cuff reading
  2. Your Check Step By Step You rest briefly, then receive a cuff measurement. The pharmacist discusses readings, risk factors and whether a further check or GP review may be advisable. Avoid caffeine beforehand if possible Loose sleeves for arm access
  3. The Screening Process Screening follows a simple sequence: preparation, measurement, interpretation and safety advice. Diagnosis and long-term treatment remain with your GP. Structured consultation Lifestyle discussion
  4. What Happens During The Check A pharmacist measures blood pressure, reviews context such as age and risk factors, and explains whether your reading suggests further action. Most checks are brief. Usually a short visit Questions about health history

sections.title: Preparing For Your Check
sections.proseHtml:
Preparing For Your Check

Preparation improves accuracy. Rest before measurement, wear loose sleeves, and bring previous readings if you already record them at home.

  • Wear loose sleeves
  • Avoid caffeine shortly beforehand
  • Rest briefly before reading
  • Bring medicines list

sections.title: Safety And Professional Standards
sections.proseHtml:
Safety And Professional Standards Pharmacy checks screen for raised readings — they do not diagnose or treat hypertension on the spot. Diagnosis and long-term management remain with your GP. Blood pressure screening is pharmacist-led A check is not a diagnosis on the spot Emergency symptoms need urgent medical care Suitability is confirmed for each patient

When To Seek GP Or Urgent Care Chest pain, severe headache, sudden vision changes or neurological symptoms require urgent medical attention — not a routine pharmacy check alone. Chest pain needs urgent medical attention Stroke symptoms need urgent medical attention A sudden severe headache needs urgent care

Professional Insight Pharmacist-led screening works best when patients understand the limits of a single reading and follow advice on when a further check or GP review may help. One reading has limits on its own White-coat effect can raise clinic readings Bring your own readings if you have them Follow the safety advice you are given

Trust And Clinical Governance Regulated pharmacy teams follow clinical governance for blood pressure screening, with a clear scope that complements GP care. Premises are regulated for pharmacy care Clinical check protocols are followed Advice can be documented for your records Pharmacy screening complements GP care

faqs.question: How are blood pressure checks arranged?
faqs.answer: Contact the pharmacy to ask how the service is arranged.

faqs.question: How long does a blood pressure check take?
faqs.answer: Most checks are brief, covering measurement and a short discussion of your reading.

faqs.question: Can a pharmacy diagnose high blood pressure?
faqs.answer: No — pharmacy checks screen for raised readings. Diagnosis and long-term treatment remain with your GP.

faqs.question: How often should I have my blood pressure checked?
faqs.answer: Frequency depends on age, risk factors and previous readings. Over-40s and those with risk factors often benefit from regular checks.

faqs.question: What should I do before my check?
faqs.answer: Rest briefly, wear loose sleeves, avoid caffeine shortly beforehand if possible, and bring any recent readings you already have.

faqs.question: What if my reading is high?
faqs.answer: A raised reading does not diagnose hypertension on its own. The pharmacist will explain what the numbers may mean and when speaking to a GP or seeking urgent care is appropriate.

faqs.question: What do systolic and diastolic numbers mean?
faqs.answer: Systolic is pressure when the heart beats; diastolic is when it rests — both are recorded in mmHg.

faqs.question: Should I bring my medicines list?
faqs.answer: Yes — some medicines affect blood pressure. Sharing your list helps the pharmacist give accurate advice.
